Its maṇḍala has the appearance of a lunar disc, surrounded by *pāṭala* flowers.
The mantra for it is:
"Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ saṃsaḥ svāhā. With this same mudrā, bend the two earth-fingers (the little fingers) into the palms; this is the Seal of the Tathāgata Adorned with Ten Thousand Virtues.
Its maṇḍala is shaped like a half-moon, encircled by the great bindu (the dot). Its mantra is:
"Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ, haṃ hoḥ, svāhā.

Furthermore, with the hands of concentration and wisdom joined in the gesture of unopened blossoms, one establishes the two space-wheels (*ākāśa-cakra*) and slightly bends them; this is the seal (*mudrā*) from which all limbs of the Tathāgata are produced.
Its maṇḍala is in the shape of a full moon, like a *kālaśa* fruit, surrounded by vajras. Its mantra is:
"Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ, aṃ, svāhā. By bending the fire-finger (*anāmikā*) of this very mudrā while the remaining characteristics remain as before, this is the World-Honored One’s dhāraṇī-mudrā.
The maṇḍala is like a rainbow, encircled on all sides by hanging vajra-banners.

Its mantra is: "Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ | buddhadhāraṇī | samudratīramaladhana-karī | dhāraya svāhaṃ | bhagavati | ākaravati | samaye | svāhā. Furthermore, with the hollow palms joined, open and spread the fire-wheel (the index fingers), while the earth-wheel (the thumbs) and space-wheel (the little fingers) are joined and held together; this is called the Tathāgata-dharmasthitimudrā.
That maṇḍala is like empty space, encircled by various colors, and marked with two *bindus*.

Its mantra is: "Namaḥ samantabuddhānām, āveśanidhi svāhā. As before, with the hollow palms joined, one empowers them with the hands of wisdom (*prajñā*) and samādhi (*samādhi*) while rotating them; this is called the Seated Lord’s Seal of Swift Retention (*bhagavataḥ kṣipra-dhāraṇī-mudrā*).
That maṇḍala is also like space, adorned with blue dots.
Its mantra is as follows:
"Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ | mahāyogayogīśvara | yogīśvari | khañjarīṭi | svāhā. O Lord of Secrets!

This is called the Tathāgata’s secret seal, the most supreme secret; it should not be bestowed upon others indiscriminately, except for those who have already received empowerment, whose nature is gentle and pliant, who are diligent and steadfast, who have made sublime vows, who revere their teachers and elders, who are mindful of their kindness and virtue, who are pure both internally and externally, and who seek the Dharma even at the cost of their own bodies and lives.

Chapter Fifteen: The Chapter on the Vidyādhara Precepts. At that time, Vajrapāṇi again addressed the World-Honored One Mahāvairocana in verse, inquiring about the precepts for vidyādharas, for the sake of those bodhisattvas who practice the bodhisattva path through the gateway of mantras.
"How does one accomplish the prohibitive precepts?
How does one abide in śīla?
How, according to where one abides, does one practice so as to be free from all attachments?"
For how many months has one practiced, until the prohibitions and precepts are brought to completion?
Abiding in what teaching does one come to know that majestic power?
How is one free from time, place, and action, as well as from dharma and non-dharma?
How may one quickly achieve success?
I pray that the Buddha will explain its measure.
As previously proclaimed by the Buddhas, it enables one to attain siddhi.
"I ask the All-Knowing One, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, for the sake of future sentient beings; may the Honored One among Benevolent Ones bear witness.
At that time, the Bhagavat Vairocana, out of compassion for sentient beings, spoke these verses:
“Excellent, O diligent hero, O Great Virtue, Vajradhara!
The sublime precepts you have proclaimed were expounded by the Buddhas of antiquity.
Precepts arising from the light of conditions, abiding in these precepts as a Perfectly Awakened One.”
To bring about the attainment of siddhi for the benefit of the world,
one should give rise to the reality of oneself, harbor no doubts or hesitations,
abide constantly in meditative equipoise, and complete the practice of the precepts.
The bodhicitta and the Dharma, together with the fruits of training and practice,
are unified as a single characteristic; being free from all conditioned activity,
one possesses the precepts like the Buddha’s wisdom— other than this, one does not possess the precepts.
Having attained mastery over all dharmas, they penetrate the ways to benefit sentient beings;
constantly practicing the conduct of non-attachment, they regard pebbles and precious jewels as equal.
Even up to a full *lakṣa*, regarding the mantra teachings that have been expounded, they remain thus.
When the time, month, and so forth have concluded, the period of the prohibitions comes to an end.
First, perform the visualization of the Golden Wheel;
abiding in the Great Indra, one should bind the Vajra Mudrā and sustain the body by drinking milk.
When the practitioner has completed one month, being able to regulate the inhalation and exhalation of the breath,
he should, in the second month, within the solemn and upright water-mandala,
employ the lotus seal to consume pure, refined water.
Next, in the third month, one practices the visualization of the supreme and wondrous wheel of fire;
by consuming food that is not sought after, one immediately uses the power of great wisdom to incinerate all sins,
thereby generating [purity] in body, mind, and speech.
In the fourth month, one practices the wind-maṇḍala;
the practitioner constantly partakes of the wind, binds the Dharmacakra mudrā, and recites with a concentrated mind.
Visualizing the Vajra-water-maṇḍala, one abides in yoga.
This is the fifth month, having distanced oneself from attainment and non-attainment.
The practitioner is without attachment, equal to *sambodhi*;
harmonizing the wheels of wind and fire, they transcend all faults and afflictions.
Furthermore, by reciting [this] for one month, while likewise renouncing both gain and loss,
the hosts of devas such as Brahmā and Śakra, as well as mahoragas and piśācas,
will dwell at a distance and pay homage; all shall provide protection.
All shall respectfully receive these instructions.
Humans, devas, yakṣas, and spirits, as well as vidyādharas and various ṛṣis,
shall attend upon his left and right, performing whatever he commands.
As for those who create obstacles through unwholesome deeds, such as rākṣasas and the seven mothers,
upon seeing one who upholds the mantra, they will revere and keep their distance.
Seeing the light at this place, they will scatter in all directions like a fierce fire.
In accordance with the teachings of the Dharma in which they dwell, And because they rely upon the clear prohibitions,
The true sons of the Samyaksaṃbuddha Attain mastery over all things.
They subdue those who are difficult to tame, Just like the Great Vajradhara.
Benefiting all living beings, you shall be equal to Avalokiteśvara.
After six months have passed, you will achieve the fruits according to your vows;
always, for both yourself and others, you should protect them with compassion.

Chapter Sixteen: The True Knowledge of the Ācārya At that time, the Vajradhara again questioned the World-Honored One Mahāvairocana regarding the heart of the mantras of all maṇḍalas, speaking in verse:
"What is the heart of the true speech of all mantras?"
How is one understood to be called an *ācārya*?
At that time, the Bhagavān Mahāvairocana consoled Vajrapāṇi: "Excellent, O Mahāsattva!"
Causing his mind to rejoice,
he further spoke these words:
"The most secret among secrets, the wisdom-mantra of the Great Mind."
I shall now proclaim it for you; listen with single-minded attention.
That which is called the syllable A is the heart of all mantras;
from it flow forth everywhere immeasurable mantras.
All conceptual proliferation ceases, And skillful wisdom is born.
Lord of Secrets, what is it That is the heart of all true speech?
The Buddha, the Honored One among bipeds, Has taught that the syllable *A* is its seed.
Therefore, all things are thus: having properly arranged and firmly established all the constituent parts, one bestows them all in accordance with the Dharma.
Through those primordial syllables, they pervade the augmented syllables.
The multitude of syllables forms sounds, and from these the limbs arise;
thus it pervades all things, and the body produces various virtues.
Now I shall explain its distribution—O Son of the Buddha, listen with a single mind.
Forming the mind with the mind, and arranging the remaining limbs accordingly—
performing everything in this manner, one becomes identical to my own essence.
Seated upon the yoga throne, one should call to mind all the Tathāgatas.
If one understands this vast wisdom within these teachings,
and the great merit of Perfect Enlightenment, such a person is called an Ācārya;
they are indeed the Tathāgata, and they are also named a Buddha.
Bodhisattvas and Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśvara,
the deities of the sun, moon, and water, Śakra, Lord of the World,
Kṛṣṇa, Yama, and others, the Earth Goddess and Sarasvatī—
The brahmins and those who constantly bathe are also called practitioners of the holy life;
the community of bhikṣus whose outflows are exhausted, who maintain auspicious secrets,
who possess all-knowing vision, and who have mastery over the wealth of the Dharma.
If one abides in the bodhicitta and the nature of sound and wisdom,
remaining unattached to all phenomena, this is called "pervading all.
Such a person is a speaker of truth, upholding the auspicious mantra.
The King of True Speech holds the Vajra seal. All the wheels of syllables,
whether they reside in the limbs or are known to abide between the eyebrows, are the *hūṃ* syllable, the vajra phrase.
The syllable *sa* resides below the lips; it is called the Lotus Phrase.
I am the very heart-position, sovereign in all places, pervading all varieties of sentient and non-sentient beings.
The syllable A is the primary life-force; the syllable Va is named water;
the syllable Ra is named fire; the syllable Hūṃ is named wrath;
the syllable Kha is identical to space, which is the so-called point of ultimate emptiness.
One who knows this as the most true reality is called an ācārya.
Therefore, one should possess skillful means and thoroughly understand what the Buddha has taught;
by constantly practicing with diligent effort, one shall attain the deathless state.
Chapter Seventeen: The Arrangement of Syllables. At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Furthermore, Secret Lord!..."
The Buddhas have proclaimed the arrangement of the various syllable-gates; O Son of the Buddha, listen with a single mind.
The syllable *ga* constitutes the neck; the syllable *gha* is in the throat. The syllable *ca* is the root of the tongue;
the syllable *cha* is in the middle of the tongue. The syllable *ja* is the tip of the tongue; the syllable *jha* is the place where the tongue arises.
The syllable *Ṭa* constitutes the shins; one should know that the syllable *Ṭha* is the thighs.
The syllable *Ṇa* is said to be the waist, and the syllable *Ta* is for the seated posture. The syllable *Tā* is the final part; one should know that the syllable *Tha* is the abdomen.
The syllable *Na* represents the two hands, the syllable *Dha* is named the flanks, and the syllable *Pa* constitutes the back.
One should know that the letter *pha* is the chest; the letter *ma* is the two elbows; the letter *ba* is next below the arms;
the letter *maṃ* dwells in the heart; the letter *ya* is the mark of the private organ;
the letter *ra* is named the eyes; the letter *la* is the broad forehead; the letters *e* and *ī* are at the two corners of the eyes; and *o* and *ū* are the two lips.
*Ī* and *Ai* are the two ears; *U* and *Au* are the two cheeks. The syllable *Aṃ* is the word for bodhi, and the syllable *Aḥ* is parinirvāṇa.
Knowing all these dharmas, the practitioner attains perfect awakening.
The wealth of omniscience always resides within their mind; thus the world calls them "Omniscient One."
This is called sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
*The Mahāvairocana-sūtra on the Empowerment of the Buddha’s Miraculous Transformations*, Scroll Five.
*The Mahāvairocana-sūtra on the Empowerment of the Buddha’s Miraculous Transformations*, Scroll [Five].
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha of Central India and the Śramaṇa Yi Xing during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Chapter 18: On Receiving the Training in Expedient Means. At that time, the Vajradhara Lord of Mysteries addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We pray that you will explain the phrases of training cultivated by the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who possess wisdom and skillful means, so that those who take refuge may have no dualistic thoughts regarding the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, may be free from doubt and hesitation, and may never be destroyed throughout the cycle of birth and death.”
Having spoken thus, the World-Honored One Vairocana surveyed the entire dharma-realm with the eye of a Tathāgata and addressed the Vajradhara Lord of Mysteries, saying:
"Listen attentively."
Vajrapāṇi! I shall now explain the path of skillful practice.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in this, they shall attain thorough penetration into the Mahāyāna.
Lord of Secrets!

A bodhisattva who observes the precept against taking life must not commit it; likewise, they must not engage in taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, harsh speech, divisive speech, or idle chatter; nor should they harbor covetousness, malice, or wrong views. All such things are improper for them to do.
Lord of Mysteries!
Regarding these phrases of training, whenever a bodhisattva practices them, they act in concert with the Perfectly Awakened World-Honored Ones and all bodhisattvas; thus should they train.
At that time, the Vajradhara Lord of Secrets addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

The Bhagavat has also taught these ten paths of wholesome action in the Śrāvaka Vehicle; furthermore, the people of the world and all the non-Buddhists also constantly aspire to practice these ten paths of wholesome action."
World-Honored One!
What is the distinction between them?
In what way are they variously different?
When he had spoken thus, the Buddha addressed the Vajradhara Lord of Mysteries, saying:
“Excellent, excellent,
Lord of Mysteries!”
It is excellent that you are able to ask the Tathāgata about such a meaning. Guhyakādhipati!
You should listen attentively; I shall now expound the dharma-gate of the differentiated paths and the single path.
"Lord of Secrets!

Regarding the training rules of the Śrāvaka vehicle, I say they are devoid of wisdom and skillful means; they are taught only to achieve and develop partial knowledge. They do not practice the ten paths of wholesome action equally, and because those worldly beings are further detached from attachment to a self, they are driven by external causes."

When a bodhisattva practices the Mahāyāna and enters into the equality of all phenomena, they embrace wisdom and skillful means; because this benefits both self and others, all their actions are transformed.
"Therefore, Lord of Mysteries!
A bodhisattva should diligently train in this gathering of wisdom and skillful means to enter into the equality of all phenomena.
At that time, the World-Honored One again gazed upon the realms of sentient beings with eyes of great compassion and addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, saying:

"Lord of Secrets! Those bodhisattvas shall maintain the precept of not taking life for as long as they live; they should lay aside the sword and staff, abandon the intent to kill, and protect the lives of others as they do their own."

There is another expedient means: among the various classes of sentient beings, according to their respective activities, one performs whatever deeds are necessary to liberate them from the retribution of evil karma, doing so without a mind of enmity or harm.
"Furthermore, Guhyapati!

A bodhisattva upholds the precept against taking what is not given; regarding all objects of enjoyment belonging to others, he does not even give rise to the thought of touching or seizing them, much less taking other things that have not been given."

There is another expedient means: seeing that sentient beings are stingy and hoarding their wealth without cultivating the merit of giving, he assumes a form similar to theirs to destroy that stinginess. Free from the distinction between self and other, he practices giving on their behalf; by praising the virtue of giving at the proper time, he causes them to obtain excellent physical forms and other such rewards.
"Lord of Secrets!
If a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of desire and grasps at it, that bodhisattva falls away from the factors of enlightenment and transgresses the unconditioned discipline (vinaya)."
"Furthermore, Guhyapati!

When a bodhisattva upholds the precept against sexual misconduct, if it concerns those who are under the protection of another—such as one's own wife, or those protected by the insignia of their own clan—they do not give rise to a mind of desire, much less engage in the union of two bodies through improper paths."
There are other skillful means by which he gathers and protects sentient beings according to their needs for deliverance.
"Furthermore, Secret Lord!

A bodhisattva maintains the precept against false speech for as long as life lasts; even for the sake of preserving his life, he should not speak falsely, for to do so would be to deceive the enlightenment of all Buddhas."
"Lord of Secrets!
This is called the Bodhisattva abiding in the supreme Mahāyāna.
If one speaks falsely, one transgresses and loses the Dharma of Buddha-enlightenment."
Therefore, O Lord of Mysteries!
You should understand this Dharma-gate in this way: abandon all untrue speech.
Furthermore, O Lord of Mysteries!
A bodhisattva who upholds the precept against harsh and abusive speech should gather in all sentient beings with gentle words and expressions appropriate to their kind. Why is this?
Lord of Mysteries!
When Bodhisattvas first practice, they act for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
Alternatively, when other Bodhisattvas see those dwelling in the causes of the evil destinies, they may manifest harsh speech in order to subdue them.
"Furthermore, Guhyapati!
A bodhisattva upholds the precept against divisive speech; he avoids words that cause estrangement and words that cause affliction and harm. One who violates this is not called a bodhisattva."

One does not give rise to a mind of alienation or division toward sentient beings; rather, there is an alternative skillful means: if those sentient beings develop attachment to whatever they perceive, one speaks words of separation according to their respective dispositions, causing them to abide in the single path—namely, the path of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
"Furthermore, Guhyakādhipati!

A bodhisattva upholds the precept against frivolous speech by employing appropriate words that accord with the circumstances and timing to produce benefit and meaning, causing all sentient beings to give rise to a joyful mind and purifying the path of their faculty of hearing."
Why is this? Because bodhisattvas employ distinct modes of speech.
Alternatively, some bodhisattvas first employ playful jesting to arouse the inclinations of sentient beings, causing them to abide in the Buddha-dharma.
Although such a bodhisattva may utter speech that is devoid of benefit, they do not become attached to the cycle of birth and death.
Furthermore, O Lord of Secrets,
a bodhisattva should maintain the precept of non-greed, and should not give rise to defiled thoughts regarding the enjoyment of others' property.
Why is this? Because there is no such thing as a bodhisattva giving rise to a mind of attachment.
If a bodhisattva’s mind possesses defiled thoughts, they will lack the power to enter the gateway of omniscience and will fall into one-sidedness.
Furthermore, Lord of Mysteries!
A bodhisattva should give rise to joy and conceive this thought:
"This is what I ought to do."
"May they arise spontaneously. "How excellent!
he thought, repeatedly congratulating himself so that those sentient beings would not suffer any loss of their resources.
"Furthermore, Guhyakādhipati!

A bodhisattva should uphold the precept of non-anger, constantly cultivating patience in all circumstances, remaining unattached to both anger and joy, and proceeding with a mind of equanimity toward both enemies and kin."
Why is this? It is not that a bodhisattva harbors malicious intent. For what reason?
Because the fundamental nature of a bodhisattva is pure,
therefore, O Lord of Mysteries,
a bodhisattva should maintain the precept of non-anger.
"Furthermore, O Lord of Secrets!

A bodhisattva should abandon wrong views and practice right view; fearing the next world, being without malice, without crookedness, and without guile, his mind should be upright and straight, and he should attain certainty in his mind regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
Therefore, Lord of Mysteries!
Wrong views constitute the most extreme fault, for they can sever all the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva; they are the mother of all unwholesome dharmas.
"Therefore, Lord of Mysteries!
Even down to a mere jest, one should not give rise to the causes and conditions for wrong views.
At that time, the Vajradhara Lord of Mysteries addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that you will expound upon the precepts of the ten paths of wholesome action, which sever [afflictions] at their very roots.

How is it that a Bodhisattva, possessing sovereign power over a royal throne, dwelling in a palace, surrounded by parents, wife, children, and retinue, may experience celestial and exquisite pleasures without giving rise to transgressions?”
When he had spoken thus, the Buddha addressed Vajrapāṇi, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Lord of Secrets!”
Listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall now expound the skillful means for determining the *vinaya* of the bodhisattvas.
Guhyakādhipati! You should know that there are two kinds of bodhisattvas.
What are these two?
They are the householder and the renunciant.
O Lord of Mysteries!

That lay bodhisattva, having received and maintained the five precepts, possesses power and sovereignty; through various skillful means (*upāya*) and in accordance with time and place, he freely gathers in those who seek all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). That is to say, being fully endowed with skillful means, he manifests himself in various arts such as teaching principles, performing dance, or serving as a master of celestial shrines (*devāyatana*), and by means of those skillful means, he gathers sentient beings through the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), causing them all to resolve to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

That is to say, upholding the precept against taking life, as well as those against taking what is not given, false speech, sexual misconduct, and wrong views—these are called the five precepts for laypeople.

A bodhisattva who upholds the well-spoken precepts should possess sincere faith and diligently train therein, following the training rules of the Tathāgatas of the past; abiding in conditioned morality and being endowed with wisdom and skillful means, they shall attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, auspicious, and unconditioned aggregate of morality.
There are four root transgressions that one must not commit, even for the sake of sustaining one's life.
What are these four? They are:
slandering the various dharmas, abandoning the bodhicitta, being stingy, and harming sentient beings.
Why is this? This nature is defiled and does not uphold the bodhisattva precepts.
For what reason?
“The Buddhas of the past, those of the future world,
and the Honored One among Men in the present— all possessing wisdom and skillful means,
they have practiced for unsurpassed enlightenment and attained the siddhi of the untainted.”
He also speaks of other precepts, Apart from the wisdom of skillful means.
One should know that the Great Hero Exhorts and advances all the śrāvakas. Chapter Nineteen:

The Exposition of the Birth of the Hundred Syllables. At that time, the World-Honored One Vairocana surveyed the entire great assembly and proclaimed the teaching of Amogha—[the teaching] for the accomplishment of all mantras according to one’s desires, [the teaching of] the Sovereign of Mantras, the King of Mantras, the Guide of Mantras, and the One of Great Majestic Virtue, who abides in the three samayas because he has perfected the three dharmas. With a wondrous voice, he addressed the powerful Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Vīravīra, listen with one-pointed attention to all the mantras, O Guide of Mantras.
Thereupon, abiding in the Samādhi of Wisdom-Birth, he spoke the mantra called "The Hundred Lights Illuminating Everywhere," which gives rise to various skillful wisdoms:
"Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ | Aṃ. The Buddha said to Vajrapāṇi:
The True King, Savior of the World, who has achieved great majestic power,
is the Perfectly Awakened One, the Muni with mastery over the Dharma.
He destroys the darkness of all ignorance, appearing everywhere like the orb of the sun.
This is my own essential nature, empowered by the Great Muni;
for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, I shall manifest miraculous transformations,
until all [beings] may give rise to [their goals] according to their thoughts and aspirations.
They are able to perform all deeds; such are the unsurpassed words of spiritual transformation.
Therefore, in every respect, one should purify the body and leave all defilements behind;
one should always diligently practice according to principle, with the aspiration for the Buddha’s Bodhi.
Chapter Twenty: The Chapter on the Correspondence with the Fruit of the Hundred Syllables. At that time, the World-Honored One Vairocana addressed the Vajradhara Lord of Mysteries, saying:
"Lord of Mysteries!
If one enters the stage of the Great Wisdom Empowerment of the World-Honored One, the Great Awakened One, one sees for oneself that one abides in the three samaya-words.
Lord of Secrets!
Upon entering the empowerment of the Bhagavat’s Great Wisdom, one manifests buddha-activities in the form of dhāraṇīs.
At that time, the Great Awakened World-Honored One, dwelling in accordance with the presence of all assemblies, performed buddha-activities and expounded the three samaya phrases.
The Buddha said:
"O Lord of Secrets!"

Contemplate the sphere of my wheel of speech, which is vast and long, pervading immeasurable worlds as a gateway of purity; manifesting according to its inherent nature, it acts as a gateway to the Dharma-realm for all types of beings, causing all sentient beings to attain joy.
Just as the present Bhagavān Śākyamuni pervades the inexhaustible realms of empty space, diligently performing buddha-works in all lands.
O Lord of Secrets!

No sentient beings are able to know that this mark of the wheel of speech of the Blessed One is an ornamental necklace from which flows the sublime sound of perfect enlightenment; it gives birth to the image of the Buddha from the womb-treasury, causing joy to arise in accordance with the dispositions and desires of sentient beings.

At that time, the World-Honored One, throughout the gateways of the ocean of immeasurable worlds and pervading the entire Dharma-realm, earnestly exhorted and inspired beings to achieve awakening, giving rise to the practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.

They take birth within the ocean of the lineage of the world-realm adorned by the matrix and spread with exquisite flowers; through various gates of purity of nature, they purify Buddha-fields and manifest the site of enlightenment to abide in the Buddha-work.
Next, one further aspires to seek the state of *samyaksambodhi*; because one knows that the mind is immeasurable, one knows that the body is immeasurable.
Because one knows that the body is immeasurable, one knows that wisdom is immeasurable.
Because one knows that wisdom is immeasurable, one knows that sentient beings are immeasurable.
Because one knows that sentient beings are immeasurable, one knows that the realm of empty space is immeasurable.
O Lord of Mysteries!
Because the mind is immeasurable, one attains the four immeasurables.
Having attained them, one achieves supreme perfect enlightenment, possesses the ten powers of knowledge, subdues the four māras, and roars the lion’s roar with fearlessness.
The Buddha spoke in verse:
"Exertion in all this is the word of the Unsurpassed Awakened One;
Regarding the training in the hundred gates, it is the mind taught by all Buddhas."

21. Chapter on the Accomplishment of the Hundred-Syllable Position, the Twenty-first. At that time, the Vajradhara Lord of Secrets, having attained what he had never experienced before, spoke these verses:
“The Buddha has taught the Mantra, the Savior of the World, Which is able to give birth to all mantras.”
O Mahāmuni, how is this known? Who is able to know from whence [these arise]?
Who produced these various mantras?
Pray, explain who it was that produced them.
The Great Hero of Diligence speaks the supreme among teachings; may he thus reveal all these aspirations.
At that time, the Blessed One, the Muni with mastery over the Dharma, was perfectly complete and all-pervasive, extending throughout every world-system.
The Omniscient One, the Honored Vairocana, declared:
"Excellent, Mahāsattva, Great Virtuous Vajrapāṇi!
I shall now explain all that is subtle, secret, and most rare."
The secret essentials of all Buddhas cannot be known by those of external paths.
If one generates compassion within the maṇḍala, receives the empowerment of the Mahāyāna,
becomes supple through disciplined conduct, and constantly benefits others out of compassion—
Those with the conditions to contemplate Bodhi can never see it;
yet they are able to know this Great Self within their own minds.
According to the state of their own minds, they abide in the dwelling place of the Teacher.
An eight-petaled lotus, born from the mind, is most exquisitely adorned;

Regarding this Dharma-gate, one should not bestow it upon others if their root-nature is unknown, with the exception of my disciples who possess the requisite marks.
I shall now expound it; you should listen with single-minded attention.

If one is born during the period of the auspicious *śubha* constellation, aspires to supreme matters, possesses subtle wisdom, constantly remembers kindness and virtue, gives rise to a heart of longing and veneration, and dwells with joy upon hearing the Dharma—whose appearance is bluish-white or white, with a broad head and long neck, a wide and level forehead, a straight nose and full cheeks, and whose features are dignified and well-proportioned—a son of the Buddha should diligently instruct such a person.
At that time, all those endowed with majestic power were filled with joy; having heard this, they received it upon their heads and upheld it with single-minded devotion.
This entire assembly, having made vast offerings adorned in various ways, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words:
“We pray that you will expound the world-saving empowered phrases within this Dharma teaching, so that the Eye of the Dharma may pervade all places and endure long in the world.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, regarding this Dharma-gate, spoke these words of empowerment and mantras:

*Namo samantabuddhānām. Sarvathā jaya-jaye | tatre tatre | yoge yoge | dharme dharme | svāhā-paye svāhā-paye | buddha-satye | dharma-satye | saṃgha-satye | hūṃ hūṃ | vīna-vī | svāhā.* When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, all the Vajradharas and the foremost Bodhisattvas, such as Samantabhadra, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they accepted it with faith and practiced accordingly.

Chapter One: The Precepts for the Practice of Mantras. Within the Ritual Sequence of Offerings, Chapter One: The Precepts for the Practice of Mantras. Homage to the Buddha Vairocana!
With eyes as pure and blossoming as blue lotuses, I shall, relying on the King of Tantras, the Mahāvairocana Sūtra, explain the various ritual procedures for making offerings.
To establish the dharma of the mantras in their proper sequence, so that one may swiftly attain accomplishment therein,
and furthermore to cause the fundamental mind to be free from defilement, I now proclaim this summary according to its essentials.
Thus, at the outset, the accomplishment of the benefit of self and others is the skillful means of supreme wisdom and aspiration;
though those skillful means are immeasurable, their successful initiation arises from faith and understanding.
Regarding the fulfillment of all excellent vows for *siddhi*, all the supreme sons of the Tathāgatas [attain this].
They faithfully believe in the forms of the mantras of those Buddhas' bodies, the various mudrās and dignified postures they maintain,
the supreme path practiced through mantras, and the Vaipulya vehicle.
Sentient beings have superior, middling, and inferior inclinations; the World-Honored One has taught the methods for their realization and cultivation.
Out of compassion for the multitudes wandering through the six realms of saṃsāra, he has expounded these teachings to benefit them accordingly.
You should therefore cultivate a resolute mind of reverence and give rise to diligent sincerity and deep faith.
If one knows the practice of subduing through the wondrous mantras within the most excellent Vaipulya vehicle,
and follows what is practiced by the sons of the Sugata— the supreme vidyādhara-specific discipline—
understanding the complete assembly of conditions and constituent parts, one shall receive the transmission of the teachings, the seal of authorization, and so forth.
Seeing such a teacher, one pays respectful homage; for the sake of benefiting others, one dwells with single-minded devotion.
One gazes upon them as if they were a World-Leader, a virtuous friend, or a close kinsman.
Arousing a most earnest and sublime intention, one provides offerings and service according to whatever is required.

Skillfully following the Master’s intent to bring him joy, and when he was being embraced by his compassion, I bowed my head and requested the Victorious Sugata to proceed, saying: "I pray that the Honored One will instruct me as is appropriate."
That master, acting with sovereign authority, establishes the wondrous and perfect maṇḍala, such as the Great Compassion Treasury; according to the ritual,
he invites [the deities] into the maṇḍala and bestows the samaya upon the disciple in accordance with their capacity,
including the fundamental mantras and mudrās of the path and the site of practice, which are personally transmitted from the mouth of the Honored One.
Having attained the samaya of victory and its protection, one should then practice exactly as it has been taught.
Now, regarding what is set forth in this sūtra— the practice of equality with the true mantras—
in order to have compassion for disciples of inferior intelligence, I shall distinguish the sequential rituals.
To the Victorious One among gods, the God of Gods, the son born from the mind of Perfect Enlightenment,
down to the seals of body and speech of the worldly gods— enter this supreme vehicle of mantras.
One should always revere and never disparage those who guide others in the conduct of the secret [mantras],
for they are able to bring great benefit to all the world; therefore, do not give rise to thoughts of abandoning them,
but should constantly and uninterruptedly fix your mindfulness upon their vast and manifold virtues.
According to one's own capacity and in accordance with what is appropriate, one should serve and make offerings to all:
to the Buddha’s assembly of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; to those who preach the gates of his teaching—the path that exhausts suffering;
to the teachers who confer the precepts and those who practice the holy life together. Toward all of them, one must never harbor thoughts of disparagement or pride.
One should skillfully observe the proper timing for what ought to be done, serving with harmony and respect.
One should not engage in the mental conduct of the foolish,
nor harbor resentment toward the Honored Ones, as the World-Honored Teacher has taught in the sūtras.

Nothing can destroy great benefit like anger; in a single moment of causal conditions, it utterly incinerates all the virtues cultivated over millions of vast eons. Therefore, one should always diligently abandon this root of what is meaningless and disadvantageous.
Fulfilling all mundane and supramundane supreme aspirations, Dispelling doubts and ultimately attaining samādhi,
The benefit of self and others arises from this; Therefore, one should protect it more dearly than one's own body or life,
Beholding it as a treasury of vast and sublime merit.
From the lowest to the least, all are kept far away; Except for those saved by diverse skillful means, they dwell within with a heart of compassion yet manifest anger.
They always cherish patience and do not look for faults; Furthermore, they are constantly endowed with great kindness and compassion.
As well as joy, equanimity, and the immeasurable minds;
through the practice of benefiting others with loving-kindness, he transforms the multitudes of living beings.

Alternatively, due to a mind corresponding to great benefit, he may set them aside for the sake of waiting for the right time; if he lacks the power to bring about extensive and vast benefit, [he does not act].
Abiding in the Dharma, one contemplates only the bodhicitta; the Buddha taught that within this all practices are complete.
One fulfills the pure dharmas of petition and confession, gathering sentient beings into the Mahāyāna, causing them to abide in and uphold [the teachings], and engage in recitation and so forth.
Together with reflection and right cultivation, the wise person restrains the six sense faculties; they should always keep the mind tranquil and practice meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The root of all unwholesome dharmas is like poison, fire, a sword, frost, or hail.
Therefore, one should distance oneself from them and not associate with them.
Furthermore, because the Buddha taught that they increase pride, one should not sit or lie upon high or luxurious beds.
To state the essential point: those possessed of wisdom should completely abandon all actions that harm themselves or others.
Now, having briefly proclaimed this in successive order, I have clarified the Sūtras spoken by the Buddha,
so that through broad understanding and realization,
certainty may arise. Furthermore, one should abandon the causes of transgression, namely, the habituation of an evil mind and indolence.
Through such false thoughts, fears, and discursive talk,
one abides correctly in the samaya; thus, hindrances and obscurations shall gradually be exhausted,
and all merits and virtues shall increase.
Contemplate this according to what is appropriate; having personally received the luminous Dharma from the Honored One, observe it with correspondence and bring it to accomplishment.
According to the sequence of rituals explained, first pay homage to the Honored One who transmits the empowerment.
I shall now explain the practices to be cultivated through the recitation of mantras.
Relying upon a suitable location according to the specific site— amidst the peaks and ridges of wondrous mountains,
or within various grottoes between two mountain ranges— one shall find peace and security at all times.
Water lilies and blue lotuses adorn the ponds everywhere; by the banks and islands of the great rivers and streams, one is far removed from the clamor of crowds and people.

There are bamboo leaves on trees that spread their branches in pleasing abundance, with many milky trees and auspicious grasses; there are no mosquitoes or gadflies, nor the sufferings of cold and heat.
Though there may be many obstacles from fierce beasts and venomous insects,
one should dwell in places where one has previously stayed and wandered— such as monasteries, stupas, aranyas, or the chambers of ancient seers— and,
according to the inclinations of one’s own mind, abandon the household life and sever all clamor and worldly affairs.
Diligently turning away from the five desires and all fetters and obsessions, one should single-mindedly and deeply delight in the flavor of the Dharma.
Nourishing the mind, one seeks *siddhi*.
Able to endure the sufferings of hunger, thirst, and fatigue, one maintains a pure livelihood with virtuous companions or even without them.
One should always keep this volume of the Sublime Dharma Sūtra with them;
possessing firm faith and understanding in the true mantras, endowed with the power of pure wisdom and the capacity for endurance,
they shall exert diligence without seeking anything of the mundane world, always delighting in steadfastness and remaining free from cowardice.
Accomplishing one's own and others' goals in this present life, not following other deities and relying on fearlessness—
one who possesses these is called a good companion.
Having established the place for accomplishment, one should first abide daily in mindfulness and wisdom.
When first arising from sleep according to the Dharma, one should eliminate all obstacles that are inexhaustible;
whatever transgressions were committed through negligence during the night, one should diligently restore purity by repenting and removing them.
With faculties stilled, endowed with compassion and a mind intent on benefiting others, one vows to deliver the infinite realms of sentient beings.
Whether one bathes according to the Dharma or does not bathe, one should ensure that body, speech, and mind are pure.
Next, in a fasting chamber or a quiet, secluded place, one should adorn it by scattering exquisite flowers and the like.
One should then place images and sublime scriptures there, or else simply bring to mind the Buddhas of the ten directions.
With mind and eyes clearly perceiving the truths,
dwelling with utmost sincerity, reverence, and single-mindedness, I cast my five limbs upon the ground in prostration and take refuge in the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the ten directions,
who throughout the three periods of time possess the ten powers and the three bodies.
I take refuge in all Mahāyāna teachings; I take refuge in the assembly of those who do not regress from bodhi;
I take refuge in the true words of all vidyās; I take refuge in all secret mudrās.
With the pure actions of body, speech, and mind, I pay reverent homage with boundless and earnest devotion.
The mantra for the ritual of prostration is as follows:
"By means of this true mantra of prostration, one is able to universally prostrate before the Buddhas of the ten directions.
With the right knee touching the ground and palms joined, one should contemplate and confess all prior sinful karma."
"Accumulated by me through ignorance, I have committed various transgressions with body,
speech, and mind; because my mind was shrouded by greed, hatred, and delusion, toward the Buddha, the True Dharma,
and the Noble Sangha, toward my parents, the two teachers, and spiritual friends, and toward immeasurable sentient beings— "[1076]
Throughout the beginningless flow of birth and death, I have committed extremely grave and inexhaustible sins.
Now, in the presence of the Buddhas of the ten directions who dwell in the present, I confess them all and vow never to commit them again.
The mantra for the expedient means of emerging from transgression is as follows:
Homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, To the treasury of the True Dharma of the three types of eternal bodies,
And to the assembly of those with the great mind of supreme vow and bodhicitta— I now take refuge in all of them perfectly.
The mantra for the skillful means of taking refuge is as follows:
"I purify this body, free from all defilements, along with the bodies, speech, and minds of the three times;
surpassing in number the dust motes of oceans of buddha-fields, I offer them to all the Tathāgatas."
The Mantra for the Expedient Means of Offering the Body:
The jewel of the supreme vow of the pure bodhicitta, I now arouse it to deliver all sentient beings,
Who are entangled by the accumulation of birth-suffering and the like, And whose bodies are harmed by ignorance.
"Rescuing, gathering, and providing refuge to bring about liberation, one should always benefit all sentient beings.
The mantra for the skillful means of generating the bodhicitta is:

I now entreat all the Tathāgatas, the Greatly Awakened Ones who save the world with their bodhicitta.
I only pray that throughout the realms of the ten directions, you will constantly let fall the rain of Dharma from great clouds.

May those dwelling as ordinary beings quickly cast off this body, which is a collection of manifold sufferings.
One shall attain the stainless state, Abiding securely in the body of the pure Dharma-realm.

Furthermore, regarding all other meritorious deeds performed, Such as reciting scriptures, walking meditation, and sitting in dhyāna—

Next, one should form the samaya-mudrā, Which is called the purification of the three paths of action.

one should join the hands of concentration and wisdom, raise both thumbs (the wheels of emptiness) together,
touch all the limbs, and recite the words of truth.

As soon as this secret mudrā is bound, One can purify the stage of the Tathāgata;
The pāramitā of the stages is fulfilled, And the realm of the path of the three dharmas is accomplished.
As for the remaining mudrās and so forth, the mantra practitioner should know them in the sequence as taught in the sūtra;
by performing these, accomplishment will be attained.
Next, one should bind the Dharmadhātusaṃbhava, the insignia of secret wisdom.
Because of purifying body, speech, and mind, it revolves throughout the entire body.
With the hands of Prajñā and Samādhi, both form vajra-fists;
the two "spaces" (thumbs) rest upon their palms, and the "wind-banners" (index fingers) are held perfectly straight.
Such is called the Dharma-realm, The secret seal of purity.
The mantra for generating the Dharma-realm says:
"Just as the self-nature of the Dharma-realm, So should one contemplate one's own body."
Or by means of true speech, he proclaims it through three turnings.
One should see that which abides in the essence of phenomena, stainless like space;
for, through the power of mantras and mudrās, the practitioner is empowered.
To cause that [realization] to become firm, one contemplates one's own vajra-body and binds the Vajrajñāna-mudrā:
the hands of śamatha and vipaśyanā are placed back-to-back, with the wheels of earth,
water, fire, and wind held by the left and right hands respectively.

one should visualize that the garments thus worn produce flames of light across the entire body.

the two voids stand side by side within the palms.
Having recited that mantra, one should contemplate the stainless syllable.

The syllable RA is brilliant white, adorned with a bindu;
like a luminous jewel upon a topknot, it is placed upon the crown of the head.
Even the multitude of karmic stains accumulated throughout a hundred eons will, by this means,
be entirely extinguished, and both merit and wisdom will be perfected.

The mantra is identical to the Dharma-realm; immeasurable multitudes of sins are eliminated.
Before long, one shall achieve accomplishment and abide on the stage of non-retrogression.

Red in color and endowed with majestic radiance, Enveloped all around by a wreath of flames.

The Great Protective Vidyā of Intolerance:
By the mere recollection of it, all the vināyakas,
the rākṣasas of hideous form, and so forth— all of them flee and disperse.
Thus, purifying the body through right action, one dwells in meditative concentration and contemplates the original Lord of Mantras;
having invited him by means of mantras and mudrās, one should first manifest the samaya.

For warding off [obstacles] and purifying, it is all done in this same way. One empowers [the offerings] with the King of Original Mantras, or visualizes the Victorious Sons of the Buddhas surrounded by immeasurable and innumerable hosts.

as it is supported by the vajra, so too is this ground.

within them, one should contemplate the Teacher and the sons of the Buddhas.
Within the water, one visualizes a white lotus with a wondrous-colored vajra stalk.
An eight-petaled lotus with stamens and filaments, naturally adorned with various jewels,
constantly emitting immeasurable light and surrounded by hundreds of thousands of other lotuses;

within his perfect halo, he universally manifests as multitudes as numerous as the atoms of infinite lands.

Relying on the aforementioned expedient means, one should empower [the practice] with mantras and secret mudrās; thereafter, with a mind intent on the gift of Dharma, one should recite Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, or recite them mentally while requesting the various devas and other deities to listen and receive them.
As it is said in the verse:
"The *Vajraśekhara Sūtra* states: 'Avalokiteśvara, the Lotus-Eyed One, Is identical to all Buddhas, With a body of inexhaustible adornment.'"
"Or else, taking any one name of the Teacher of the World, the Sovereign of all Dharmas,
one should perform the empowerment of the fundamental nature.
The seed-syllable heart-mantra of Avalokiteśvara is as follows:
The true meaning of the gateway of syllables is that all phenomena are free from defilement and attachment;
one should contemplate them as emerging from sound.
Within this, the characteristic of the secret body is what is known as the lotus seal.
As previously explained in the offering of the seat, I have already analyzed and described it.
Next, the mantra of Avalokiteśvara is recited as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ | sarvatathāgatavajrotpanna-karuṇāmaya-rara-ra-hūṃ jaḥ svāhā* || One should first place the syllable of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) at the crown of the head.
Furthermore, having applied this mantra and mudrā, one should recite the sūtras and dharmas according to one's capacity, or construct a caitya, maṇḍala, or the like.
When these tasks are completed, one should next rise from one’s seat and engage with others in a manner characterized by harmony and respect.

Furthermore, in order to provide support for the physical body, one should next practice begging for food; whether by invitation from a donor or obtained within the Sangha, one should abstain from fish, meat, and pungent vegetables.

Furthermore, after making offerings to one's tutelary deity and the Buddhas, one must not consume any leftovers, including various types of stale or impure food, nor any fermented liquors, juices from wood or fruit, or any other beverages capable of causing intoxication.
Next, present the morsel of food to offer to the Honored One.
Then, perform the ritual for eating at will.
If there is still a remainder, set aside a small portion for the purpose of providing relief to those who are hungry and destitute.
One should give rise to this thought:
"I partake of this solid food in order to sustain this physical vessel so that I may practice the Path in peace and security, just as one greases the axle of a cart to prevent it from breaking down."

When arriving at any destination, one should not allow the mind to fluctuate or become attached due to the taste of food, nor should one give rise to the appearance of beautifying the body with such flavors; rather, one should then contemplate the syllable *Citta* within the *dharmadhātu* to purify all food, and empower one's own person with the Karma-vajra.
The seed syllable therein is as described in the mantra of the letter *vaṃ*.
Furthermore, one should recite the mantra for bestowing the ten powers eight times before consuming it.
This mantra is stated as follows:
*Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānām | Oṃ māranirjetirmāriṇi svāhā.* In this manner, one abides in the preliminary accomplishment of the yoga of the *iṣṭadevatā*.
When the meal is finished, one should offer the remaining *sparśāhāra* (tactile food) to those who are to be fed by means of the heart-mantra of the *Sarvakarmasādhana*.

One should employ the mantra of the Noble Acala, the Unfailing Wrathful Increaser, and recite it once; the recipient will rejoice and shall constantly follow and protect the practitioner with mindful care.
The mantra is as follows:
"Namaḥ samantavajrāṇām | Traṭ amogha | Caṇḍa mahāroṣaṇa | Sphoṭaya hūṃ | Tramaya tramaya | Hūṃ traṭ phaṭ. Having finished eating, he rested for a short while.
Furthermore, one should prostrate to all Buddhas and repent for all transgressions in order to purify the mind.
Thus, one should cultivate these regular practices, continuing even to the recitation of the scriptures as before, remaining constantly established therein.
On the subsequent day, one should likewise practice in this manner; from the first watch of the night until the last, one should contemplate the Mahāyāna without interruption.
Upon reaching the middle watch of the night, one should don the vajra armor as previously described with the *karmavajra*, and pay homage to all Buddhas, great bodhisattvas, and so forth.
Next, one should direct the mind to perform a formal offering and form this thought:

"For the sake of all sentient beings and my aspiration for the causal conditions of the Great Matter, I ought to cherish and protect this body; I shall rest briefly, not out of attachment to the pleasure of sleep."
"First, one should rectify the bodily deportment, placing the two feet one upon the other and lying on the right side.
If the limbs become weary or relaxed, there is no fault in turning over as one pleases."
To ensure one awakens quickly, one should always fix the mind on light.
Furthermore, one should not lie prostrate upon the bed.
On subsequent days, one should practice in this same manner.
Because the mantra-holder practices with unflagging regularity and uninterrupted diligence, they receive the title of "one who cultivates the bodhisattva path through the gateway of mantras.

If, while performing the preliminary preparations for the methods of recitation during the manifestation of the numerical signs, one does not achieve success despite fully cultivating superior practices, one should awaken oneself and redouble one's diligence. One must not entertain inferior thoughts, saying, "This dharma is not suitable for me."
Thus, by expanding one's resolve and power, the benefit of oneself and others is never in vain.

Because the practitioner is diligent, sincere, and unceasing, the various sages illuminate their mind with profound insight; they then receive the empowerment of majestic spiritual power to become established and free from all obstacles.
Within this, there are two matters that should not be abandoned: namely, not forsaking the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and maintaining a mind that seeks to benefit inexhaustible sentient beings.
One’s resolve for omniscience must never waver; by these causes and conditions, one will certainly attain the *siddhi* appropriate to one's kind.
One should always bathe according to the internal Dharma; one should not cling to external methods of purification.
To harbor doubts or regrets regarding the food of touch and so forth—such things as these should not be done.
If, for the sake of maintaining this body, one bathes at the appropriate times to remove all impurities,
following the instructions of the Dharma regarding rivers and other sites, in conjunction with mantras and mudrās.
Purify all waters with the mind of the *dharmadhātu*; according to their use, remain unmoving as Trailokyavijaya.
With mantras and secret mudrās, protect the directions and the equal [realms], abiding in the contemplation of the essential nature of the deity.
Furthermore, one should maintain the purity of the Buddha-land through three revolutions, Always with single-minded correct contemplation;
Reciting the Mantra of the Holy Immovable One and others, The wise person should silently perform the ritual ablution.
The seed-syllable of the Pure Dharma-realm Mind and the seed-syllable and sword-mudrā of Acala are all as previously described.
Regarding the seed-heart-mantra of Trailokyavijaya, it says:
"In this context, the 'Ha' gate—its phonetic principle is as previously described."
The slight distinction is that which is called the purification of signs.
The Honored One who subdues the three realms, through the ritual of the secret body,
should employ the five-wisdom vajra-mudrā to accomplish all activities.
Next, the mantra of Trailokyavijaya is proclaimed:
Having thus bathed and performed the ritual sprinkling for purification, and having equipped oneself with the samaya protection of the limbs,
one should contemplate the assembly of inexhaustible noble deities and offer water three times by cupping it in both hands.
To purify body and mind for the sake of benefiting others, I pay homage to the supreme sons born of the Tathāgata,
who have distanced themselves from the three poisons, conceptual discrimination, and the like, and who have calmed and disciplined their faculties to enter the chamber of refinement.
Alternatively, relying on the water-chamber as a distinct expedient means, the mind abides according to the ritual previously prescribed;
taking the three equalities of one's own body as the limit, this is for the sake of seeking the superior, middling, and inferior dharmas.
When the practitioner performs recitation in this manner, all streams of sin shall be forever stilled;
they will certainly achieve the destruction of all obstacles, and the syllables of omniscience will gather within their body.
Based on the "Chapter on Worldly Accomplishment," or as taught in other sūtras,
one practices the various skillful means of the branches of worship according to their proper sequence;
because these do not transcend the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), this is called worldly *siddhi*.
Next, the signless [practice] is explained as most supreme, observed by those possessed of faith and understanding.
For one of profound wisdom in the Mantra Vehicle who aspires in this life for the unsurpassed fruit,
they should cultivate contemplation according to their own faith and understanding, following the previously described ritual for mental offerings.
Furthermore, according to the *Siddhi-niṣyanda-paṭala* and the yogic methods of the *Lokottara-paṭala*,
one should practice and realize through these skillful means that which pertains to the phrases of true dependent origination,
wherein the internal mental factors are detached from objective referents; thus, one shall constantly attain supramundane accomplishment.
As stated in the Udāna verse:
"The profound dharma of signlessness Is beyond the capacity of those with inferior wisdom;
To accommodate them, The teaching of signs is also maintained."
